problems.description: PUT /tasks/<id> on a nonexistent task now silently creates it (upsert) and, when no title is given, returns 200 {} — replacing the prior 404 contract with ambiguous semantics that hide not-found conditions from callers.

Business logic (title normalization + create fallback) is inlined in the edit_task route handler rather than a service/repository layer; consistent with the +8 cognitive complexity delta reported by SonarQube.

The new tests intentionally codify the silent-200 and upsert behaviors (test_put_nonexistent_task_without_title_silent), locking in the questionable contract instead of asserting explicit 404 semantics.
Convention score 0.71 is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py); this commit itself adds little new convention debt.

strengths: get_db now reads app.config.get('DATABASE', DATABASE), enabling per-test isolated DBs via Flask config — a clean, idiomatic testability improvement.
Comprehensive 200-line pytest suite (~20 tests) with correct tempfile fixture teardown and config/env cleanup, keeping state from leaking across tests.
Strong edge-case coverage: empty/whitespace titles, extra fields ignored, idempotent PUT, and content-type assertions.
SonarQube reports zero new bugs, zero smells, and 0% duplication on the commit.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive session-1 commit that adds strong test coverage and a config-driven DB path for testability, though the new upsert/silent-200 PUT semantics and inline route logic introduce minor maintainability debt and obscure the previous not-found contract.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-do-not-use-in-prod' value; production should require the env var instead of silently defaulting.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12; should use datetime.now(timezone.utc).
Schema migration done via ALTER TABLE inside a try/except in init_db() is fragile; acceptable for a single-file app but not durable across sessions.

strengths: Passwords hashed with bcrypt rather than stored in plaintext.
JWT auth with expiration and a clean Flask require_auth decorator using g.user_id.
All task queries scoped by owner_id (list, get, update), closing IDOR-style cross-user access.
Follows the existing single-file Flask structure: model functions + routes, snake_case naming, get_db() pattern preserved.
Correct HTTP semantics: 400/401/404/409 for register/login/task endpoints.
commit_reviews.summary: Adds sound per-user auth (bcrypt + JWT) with owner-scoped task isolation that fits the existing single-file Flask structure, though the 0.71 measured convention score is largely driven by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_*.py, repositories.py, test_app.py) rather than this diff, which itself adds only minor debt like a hardcoded dev secret fallback and deprecated utcnow().

problems.description: Notification side-effect logic lives inside the edit_task route instead of a service/model layer, increasing route responsibility and cognitive complexity (+17 per SonarQube).

Introduces Celery + Redis broker (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) as new infrastructure for an app built on a single SQLite database, while the email task is only a placeholder print — heavyweight dependency for an unimplemented feature.
get_user_by_id uses SELECT * and returns dict(row), exposing password_hash to any caller; a focused column projection would avoid leaking credentials.
auth_headers_with_email fixture duplicates the existing auth_headers fixture rather than extending it, adding test duplication (+2 imports, 469+ lines of new tests).

Module-level Celery config values (broker_url, result_backend, timezone) and celery_app are flagged as UPPER_CASE/PascalCase violations; snake_case is idiomatic for Celery config, so several of the 8 flagged violations are nominal rather than real.

strengths: Clean integration seam: notify_task_completion with a lazy import of celery_tasks avoids circular-import issues.
Correct edge-case handling — email only fires on the status transition to 'completed', not on title-only updates — with tests covering all three paths.
Migration in init_db follows the existing guarded ALTER TABLE pattern used for owner_id.
New behavior is fully unit-tested by mocking the notification boundary.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-seamed notification integration that fits the app's existing route/get_db patterns and is well tested, but adds heavyweight Celery/Redis infrastructure for a placeholder task and embeds side-effect logic in the route.

problems.description: Password hashing moved into UserRepository.create while verify_password remains a free function in app.py, splitting the bcrypt concern across two layers.
user_repo/task_repo are module-level singletons bound to app's get_db at import time in app.py; a factory or lazy init would improve testability and decouple repo lifetime from app import.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +4, mostly from the added find_all_paginated method (cursor/total handling), which is slight scope creep beyond a pure extraction.

Reported violations for app.py (Classes should use PascalCase) and repositories.py (Module-level constants UPPER_CASE) do not obviously match the diff — neither file introduces class definitions or module constants — flagging as likely false positives; the other 5 violations are in untouched celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py/test_app.py and predate this commit.

strengths: Clean extraction of all SQL into per-entity repository classes, removing ~115 lines from app.py and centralizing data access behind a repository seam.
BaseRepository's shared _fetch_one/_fetch_all/_execute_write helpers eliminate duplication across entities.
Behavior preserved 1:1: identical SQL, HTTP status codes, error semantics, and the notification flow; SonarQube reports zero new bugs, smells, or duplications.
Consistent method naming (create/find_by_id/find_by_username/find_all/exists/update) with type hints on public signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: A disciplined, behavior-preserving repository-layer extraction that reduces duplication and improves separation of concerns with only minor debts (module-level singletons and bcrypt split across layers), though the sub-0.8 convention score is driven mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than new ones.

problems.description: Adds the flask-limiter dependency and defaults rate-limit storage to redis://localhost:6379/0, making Redis a runtime requirement, yet no requirements/pyproject change appears in the diff (an env override and memory:// for tests soften the impact).
@limiter.limit('100 per minute') is duplicated across six routes instead of a centralized default-limit/scope configuration, risking drift in limits and headers.
The /tasks GET response contract changes from a bare list to {"data", "next_cursor", "total"} — a breaking API change with no versioning or migration path.
Cognitive complexity increased by +91 per SonarQube, concentrated in the new pagination method and rate-limit test loops, adding sustained review/maintenance surface.
Pagination edge cases (empty page, exactly-at-limit boundary, cursor beyond last id, limit clamping) are not exercised by the visible tests.

The 0.71 convention score is largely driven by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py); the code introduced in this diff follows snake_case/PascalCase conventions.

strengths: User-scoped rate-limit key (g.user_id) with IP fallback is a well-designed, correct approach for per-user quotas
Keyset pagination (ORDER BY id DESC, id < cursor, fetch limit+1) avoids OFFSET inefficiency on SQLite
Thorough rate-limit tests cover 429 body, Retry-After header, memory:// storage, and a limiter.reset() autouse fixture
Consistent 429 JSON error handler and new repo method reuse the existing _fetch_one/_fetch_all patterns
New code and tests mirror the existing class-based test structure and repository conventions
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cross-cutting hardening (user-scoped rate limiting, keyset pagination) that respects existing patterns and ships with good tests, but adds +91 cognitive complexity and a Redis runtime dependency while the 0.71 convention score largely reflects pre-existing violations in untouched celery files rather than this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 1's 'update-as-upsert' PUT semantics (create a task when title is non-empty on a missing task) introduced a non-standard API behavior that persisted through later sessions.
Sessions 2-3 added auth, per-user scoping, and celery notification logic directly into the app.py monolith, accumulating tech debt that required the Session 4 repository extraction to unwind.
Session 5's rate limiter defaults to a Redis storage URL, adding a runtime dependency the earlier sessions never needed; correctness now depends on Redis availability or env override.
JWT/bcrypt auth was wired in Session 2 before any structure existed for data-access separation, so authorization logic had to be re-plumbed twice (Session 4 refactor).
key_decisions: Adopting Flask + SQLite as the baseline stack in the seed, which shaped every later session.
Introducing JWT-based auth with bcrypt and per-user task scoping in Session 2 (greenfield → feature), committing early to an authenticated multi-tenant model.
Adding async celery task integration in Session 3 to decouple email notifications from request handling.
Extracting UserRepository/TaskRepository into repositories.py in Session 4, separating data access from route handlers and shrinking app.py.
Adding flask_limiter rate limiting with a per-user key function and cursor-based pagination in Session 5 as cross-cutting concerns.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 fixed seed defects and added a real test suite (200 lines); Session 2 grew the app substantially with secure auth and user-scoped tasks alongside a much larger test suite; Session 3 layered in async celery integration; Session 4 was a clean architectural refactor that reduced app.py by roughly two-thirds while extracting a repository layer — showing the earlier monolith was consolidated rather than abandoned; Session 5 rounded out the app with rate limiting and pagination implemented through the newly-extracted repository API. The progression greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting is textbook, and each session's work is directly consumed by the next, with tests growing in lockstep the whole way.
story_review.summary: A textbook multi-session progression where early monolithic growth was repaid by a mid-story refactor, and cross-cutting concerns in the final session landed cleanly on the restructured repository layer.
